ai.text:
The HEIRS Act of 2025 would let the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) give grants to help people deal with the legal steps involved in inheriting certain real estate. The bill sets up two grant programs, and both end seven years after the law is enacted.

The first program is for states that have adopted the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act (UPHPA) or a similar state law. That law protects people who inherit property without a will from having it forced into a sale. Under older state rules, such heirs became co-owners, and any one of them could demand a partition and sell the property. Grant recipients must use the money to help residents pay for costs of proving ownership or settling an estate. Covered costs include title reports, title abstracts, copies of public records, land surveys, estate planning, heirs searches or tracing services, and recording, filing, notary, and legal fees.

The second program provides grants to housing counseling agencies, legal services clinics at colleges and universities, and qualified nonprofits. These groups must use the funds to offer housing counseling, legal help, and financial assistance for clearing titles and keeping homes for people who inherit property as co-owners.

summary.text:
Heirs Estate Inheritance Resolution and Succession Act of 2025 or the HEIRS Act of 2025
This bill authorizes the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to provide grants to assist individuals with the legal processes associated with inheriting certain real property.
Under the first program, HUD may provide grants to states that have enacted the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act (UPHPA) (or similar state law). The UPHPA provides due process protections against forced property sales for individuals who inherit real property from a landowner without a will. Historically, state property laws have provided that recipients of such property become tenants-in-common, which permits a single tenant to exercise their right to partition and sell the property.
A state, tribe, or local government must use grant funds to assist residents in the jurisdiction with expenses related to establishing and documenting property ownership rights or settling a decedent's estate, including costs related to
obtaining title reports, title abstracts, copies of public records, and land surveys;
estate planning;
heirs searches or tracing services; and
recording and filing fees, notary fees, and legal fees and expenses.
Under the second program, HUD may provide grants to housing counseling agencies, legal services clinics at institutions of higher education, and qualified nonprofits. Such organizations must use grant funds to provide housing counseling, legal assistance, and financial assistance related to title clearing and home retention efforts for individuals who inherit property as tenants-in-common.
Both grant programs terminate seven years after the enactment of this bill.
